Each inquiry anchors its analysis to a different moment in a system's lifecycle-delegation, harm, and design, respectively. For conventional tools this temporal separation is harmless because a single human actor typically occupies all three positions at once. Autonomous systems break that coincidence: the interval between design, delegation, and harm now contains machine-generated intervening choices that no human actor directly authorized, observed, or could fully anticipate. This article develops the thesis that recent liability reforms-the European Union's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the United Kingdom's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the Republic of Korea's Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, and Brazil's pending Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023)-each stabilize only one of these three temporal anchors without reconciling how the anchors interact when a single harm implicates all three simultaneously. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis across these four jurisdictions plus United States tort doctrine, the article identifies this structural problem as temporal anchor divergence: the three liability inquiries increasingly point to different responsible parties for the same harm rather than converging on one, and current reforms treat this divergence as an implementation detail rather than a problem requiring an explicit resolution rule. The article's original contribution is the Temporal Anchor Convergence Stan…

{"url": "https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.1515", "scope": "extracted web-page text; may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Where Confabulation Lives: Latent Feature Discovery in LLMs - ACL Anthology
Where Confabulation Lives: Latent Feature Discovery in
LLM
s
Thibaud Ardoin
,
Yi Cai
,
Gerhard Wunder
Abstract
Hallucination remains a critical failure mode of large language models (LLMs), undermining their trustworthiness in real-world applications. In this work, we focus on confabulation, a foundational aspect of hallucination where the model fabricates facts about unknown entities. We introduce a targeted dataset designed to isolate and analyze this behavior across diverse prompt types. Using this dataset, and building on recent progress in interpreting LLM internals, we extract latent directions associated with confabulation using sparse projections. A simple vector-based steering method demonstrates that these directions can modulate model behavior with minimal disruption, shedding light on the inner representations that drive factual and non-factual output. Our findings contribute to a deeper mechanistic understanding of LLMs and pave the way toward more trustworthy and controllable generation. We release the code and dataset at
https://github.com/Thibaud-Ardoin/where-confabulation-lives
.

id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1811.04122v1
published: 2018-11-09T20:08:58Z
summary: Testing in Continuous Integration (CI) involves test case prioritization, selection, and execution at each cycle. Selecting the most promising test cases to detect bugs is hard if there are uncertainties on the impact of committed code changes or, if traceability links between code and tests are not available. This paper introduces Retecs, a new method for automatically learning test case selection and prioritization in CI with the goal to minimize the round-trip time between code commits and developer feedback on failed test cases. The Retecs method uses reinforcement learning to select and prioritize test cases according to their duration, previous last execution and failure history. In a constantly changing environment, where new test cases are created and obsolete test cases are deleted, the Retecs method learns to prioritize error-prone test cases higher under guidance of a reward function and by observing previous CI cycles. By applying Retecs on data extracted from three industrial case studies, we show for the first time that reinforcement learning enables fruitful automatic adaptive test case selection and prioritization in CI and regression testing.

summary: This article presents novel designs of autonomous UAV prototypes specifically developed for inspecting GPS-denied tunnel construction environments with dynamic human and robotic presence.
